chapters.title: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation

concepts.text: Indus Valley/Harappan civilisation named after Harappa, the first site discovered
Meaning of 'culture' in archaeology: a group of objects of a distinct style found together in an area and period
Mature Harappan period c. 2600-1900 BCE; Early and Late Harappan phases
Map work: major Harappan sites (Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi, Banawali, Chanhudaro, Shortughai, Nageshwar, Balakot)
Early Harappan cultures preceded the mature phase in the same region
Break between early and mature phases: burnt layers and abandonment of some sites
Diet: plants and animal products including fish; evidence from charred grains and seeds
Crops: wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice rarer
Animal bones of cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo, pig; wild species (boar, deer, gharial)
Uncertain whether Harappans hunted or obtained meat from hunting communities
Agricultural technologies: terracotta plough models, ploughed field at Kalibangan
Use of bulls for ploughing; furrows criss-crossing for two crops
Irrigation: canals at Shortughai, wells, reservoirs at Dholavira
Tools for harvesting: stone blades, metal tools (debated)
Settlement divided into a raised Citadel and a larger Lower Town
Buildings on platforms; planning done before construction
Standardised brick ratio (length:breadth:height = 4:2:1) across sites
Laying out drains: grid-pattern roads with covered drains; house drains linked to street drains
Domestic architecture: courtyard houses, no windows on ground floor walls facing streets, privacy
Bathrooms paved with brick, wells in many houses, staircases to upper floors
The Citadel: warehouse (granary) and the Great Bath with steps and side rooms
Great Bath as a possible ritual bathing place
Sources activity: reading a site plan of Mohenjodaro
Burials: pits lined with bricks; pottery and ornaments in some graves
Variation in burial goods shows some social differences but not extreme ones
Looking for 'luxuries': classification into utilitarian and luxury artefacts
Faience pots and rare materials found in large cities; gold hoards
Chanhudaro as a craft-production centre: bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making, weight-making
Bead materials: carnelian, jasper, crystal, quartz, steatite, copper, bronze, gold, shell, faience, terracotta
Bead-making techniques: grinding, polishing, drilling; firing to produce red carnelian
Shell objects at Nageshwar and Balakot (bangles, ladles, inlay)
Identifying centres of production through raw material, tools, unfinished objects, waste
Materials from the subcontinent: bullock carts and river routes
Settlements near sources: Nageshwar and Balakot (shell), Shortughai (lapis lazuli), Lothal (carnelian, steatite)
Expeditions to Khetri (Rajasthan) for copper and South India for gold
Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture as copper source
Contact with distant lands: copper from Oman, Magan; Mesopotamian texts mention Dilmun, Magan, Meluhha
Meluhha possibly the Harappan region; goods like carnelian, lapis lazuli, gold, timber
Persian Gulf seals and sea trade evidence
Seals and sealings used to secure long-distance communication and goods
Harappan seals made of steatite with animal motifs and signs
An enigmatic script: undeciphered, written right to left, 375-400 signs
Script not alphabetic; short inscriptions on seals, copper tools, pots
Weights: chert, cubical, no markings; binary system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...) for lower and decimal for higher denominations
Use of weights for precious metals and trade
Evidence of complex decisions: standard bricks, planned settlements, craft organisation
Palaces and kings: no conclusive palace; 'priest-king' statue as a speculative label
Theories: no single ruler, several rulers, or a single state
By c. 1800 BCE most mature sites abandoned in Cholistan and elsewhere
Expansion of new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana, western UP
Changes in material culture: disappearance of seals, script, specialised beads, weights
Possible causes: climate change, deforestation, floods, shifting rivers, overuse of landscape
Collapse of a unifying state as one explanation
Cunningham's confusion: first DG of ASI, guided by Chinese pilgrims' accounts and early historic period
Cunningham could not fit Harappan seals into the known chronology
A new old civilisation: Daya Ram Sahni (Harappa) and R.D. Banerji (Mohenjodaro) found seals in the 1920s
John Marshall announced a new civilisation in 1924
Marshall's horizontal excavation method ignoring stratigraphy
R.E.M. Wheeler's stratigraphic method
After Partition: new sites found in India and Pakistan
New techniques and questions: scientific analysis, studies of plant and animal remains

Urban populations: elites and craftspersons; Northern Black Polished Ware
Donative inscriptions listing washing folk, weavers, scribes, carpenters, potters, goldsmiths

sections.name: 3.1 Introduction and The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata

Palaces with stone platforms, water tanks and stepped tank

concepts.text: Looking for sources: Ain-i Akbari by Abu'l Fazl as the main source; revenue records of Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan; EIC records

New crops from the New World: maize, tomatoes, potatoes, chillies, pineapple, papaya

Three constituents: cultivators, panchayats, village headman

Panchayats and headmen: assembly of elders; muqaddam or mandal

Women petitioning panchayats against husbands
Beyond settled villages: forests (jangli) covered large areas

chapters.title: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives

concepts.text: Colonial rule's impact on rural society through revenue policies

chapters.title: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations

concepts.text: Revolt began in Meerut on 10 May 1857 with sepoys' mutiny, then spread to Delhi

Targets: government buildings, jails, offices, records; British officials and their families

Rumours and prophecies: greased cartridges (cow and pig fat), bone dust in flour, end of British rule after 100 years of Plassey
